opening_message:
Ticket 1: Keith Mclaughlin (employee ID E032) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E032.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Keith Mclaughlin (E032), Analyst, full-time employee, requests write access to Source Code. Full-time employees may have up to write access (admin requires owning role; Analyst does not own Source Code). Requested level is within policy, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E032 is a contractor with basic security training (HR note listed full-time; Security DB is authoritative here). Contractors with basic training max out at read; write requires advanced training. Recommend read.

Contractors with basic training max out at read access to Source Code. The requested write level exceeds the maximum, so I grant the maximum allowed level: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: Keith Mclaughlin (E032)
Request: write access to Source Code

There's a conflict between HR and Security notes:
- HR says: full_time employee, Analyst, recommend write
- Security says: contractor with basic security training, recommend read (Security DB is authoritative)

According to the policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns the system.
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Security says the Security DB is authoritative: E032 is a contractor with basic training. So max = read (contractors with basic training max out at read).

Requested level is write, which is above the maximum (read). So grant the maximum = read.

Never grant more than the requested level - read is less than write, fine.

So decision: read.

Submit decision with reason.
